title: An Illinois Prison Drove Desperate Men to Set Themselves on Fire
why: Records show more than 70 fires and two deaths at Illinois’ Joliet Treatment Center, a prison for men with serious mental illness, where staff repeatedly failed to prevent or respond as men set themselves ablaze — exposing how the state warehouses rather than treats incarcerated people in crisis.

title: KC neighborhood leaders ponder Housing Trust Fund
why: Kansas City voters will decide an Aug. 4 ballot measure on a $100 million bond for the city’s Housing Trust Fund, and neighborhood leaders are weighing whether the money will actually reach the low-income residents facing the steepest housing costs.

title: Jason Ellsworth’s big do-over
why: A day after a jury convicted former Montana Senate President Jason Ellsworth of official misconduct, a clerical error that exposed jurors to sealed exhibits wiped out the verdict — resetting a marquee public-corruption case and raising the prospect of a retrial.

title: Data center company decides not to build in East Texas
why: Diode Ventures scrapped a planned East Texas data center, citing Gov. Greg Abbott’s new push to curb rural data-center growth — an early sign the AI build-out straining water and power in Texas and other states may be hitting political limits.

title: Can Wisconsin voters void a returned absentee ballot? New lawsuit sends issue back to court
why: New state guidance says Wisconsin voters can’t cancel an absentee ballot once it’s returned, and three voters are suing — a dispute over ballot rules that courts in battleground states often look to as precedent heading into the fall elections.

title: EPA violated key soot standard in Clean Air Act, court rules
why: A federal judge found the EPA broke the Clean Air Act by missing its legal deadline to flag communities that fail the 2024 soot standard — a ruling that determines whether millions of people in polluted areas get the cleanup protections the law promises.

title: Darrell Hines’ attorneys seek to ID doctor ahead of execution
why: Lawyers for a man set to be executed Aug. 13 are fighting Tennessee’s secrecy laws to learn whether a physician will oversee the lethal injection — a test of how much the public is allowed to know about how states carry out executions.

title: Adams opts Kentucky into ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ scholarship tax credit program
why: Kentucky will join a new federal tax-credit program that funnels money to private-school scholarships — a decision states are weighing one by one that redirects potential tax revenue toward private education and reshapes school-choice funding.

title: ICE is arresting relatives who come forward to take custody of migrant children in federal shelters
why: A new federal practice lets ICE arrest parents and relatives who step forward to claim children held in government shelters; advocates say it turns detained kids into “bait,” leaving more minors stuck in custody and discouraging families from reuniting.

title: Colorado town sued over ICE detention center
why: An immigrant-rights group sued the town of Hudson to block a shuttered private prison from becoming an ICE detention center, arguing the site isn’t zoned for it — a local zoning fight that could slow the administration’s push to expand detention capacity.

title: Vermont to give local news priority for state advertising dollars
why: Gov. Phil Scott signed an order steering state advertising to Vermont-based news outlets first — a small but replicable model other states could copy to shore up struggling local newsrooms as commercial ad revenue keeps collapsing.

title: 911 call times are slow. Do San Diego County supervisors care?
why: An investigation finds San Diego County’s 911 calls routinely miss target answer times while county supervisors show little urgency to fix it — a lag that can decide life-or-death outcomes when residents call for help.

title: Gov. Cox declares state of emergency as majority of Utah under flood watch
why: Days of flash flooding pushed Gov. Spencer Cox to declare a state of emergency in Beaver, Piute and Sevier counties with most of Utah under a flood watch, freeing state resources as rural communities brace for more damage.

title: Independent autopsy on Nolan Xavier Wells is inconclusive, can't rule out foul play
why: An independent pathologist hired by attorney Ben Crump said he could not rule out foul play in the death of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, whose body was found near Mississippi's Horn Island, keeping a nationally watched case open and pressing authorities to reinvestigate.

title: Ellsworth guilty verdict thrown out
why: A judge tossed the official-misconduct conviction of former Montana Senate President Jason Ellsworth after learning jurors were mistakenly handed sealed exhibits, reopening a high-profile public-corruption case just a day after the jury found him guilty.

title: Cancer research could stall amid Texas' limits on foreign workers
why: Texas spent billions building MD Anderson into a global cancer-research hub by recruiting hundreds of foreign-born scientists; new state and federal limits on H-1B workers now threaten to halt studies and push researchers to other states and countries.

title: Pair of Kentucky chemical plants exempted from EPA rule meant to reduce harmful emissions
why: The Trump administration gave a Louisville and a Calvert City chemical facility at least two more years to meet federal limits on toxic emissions, part of a wave of exemptions that leaves nearby residents exposed to hazardous pollutants for longer.

title: State budget provision ends local inclusion requirements in public contracting
why: A provision tucked into North Carolina's new budget bars local governments from requiring minority- and women-owned business participation in public contracts, a change that could reshape who wins millions of dollars in government work statewide.

title: Colorado's historic snow drought was made 14 times more likely by climate change, study finds
why: A Colorado School of Mines study found this year's severe Upper Colorado River Basin snow drought was 14 times more likely because of long-term warming, a finding with direct stakes for the roughly 40 million people across seven states who depend on the river's water.

title: Louisville voters got wrong ballots. Kentucky officials say statewide accuracy will take money
why: After LPM found more than 2,100 Louisville households may have received wrong ballots for years, Kentucky election officials acknowledged that fixing precinct-mapping errors statewide will require new funding, an accountability gap that determines who can vote in which races.

title: After CPS Closed Schools, Buildings Sat Empty — And Gun Violence Rose, Study Finds
why: A new study found gun violence rose around the Chicago public schools shuttered and left vacant after the 2013 mass closures, while reused buildings saw less, evidence that bears directly on how cities nationwide dispose of empty school properties.

title: Project Jupiter's $50 million water fund could begin flowing next year
why: The $50 million a data-center developer pledged for water infrastructure in Sunland Park and Santa Teresa may finally reach Doña Ana County next year after officials sought state help tracking it, a test of whether communities can hold data centers to their water promises.

title: Jury finds Ellsworth guilty of official misconduct
why: A Helena jury convicted former state Senate President Jason Ellsworth of steering $170,000 in no-bid contracts to a business associate, a rare criminal accountability verdict against a top Montana lawmaker who now faces up to six months in jail.

title: Federal appeals court overturns Vermont judge's ruling that released Mohsen Mahdawi
why: A U.S. appeals court held that the Vermont judge lacked authority to free the Columbia student and pro-Palestinian activist from immigration custody, a ruling with national implications for whether courts can check ICE detention of activists.

title: State elections expert confirms voting assignment issues in Louisville
why: A State Board of Elections review found 2,186 Louisville addresses whose precinct assignments can't be verified against digital maps, corroborating LPM reporting that voters may have received the wrong ballots for years.

title: Chickenpox exposures triggered ICE Camp East Montana quarantine
why: A chickenpox outbreak forced a weeks-long quarantine at the El Paso-area ICE tent facility, exposing how disease spreads in crowded immigration detention camps and how slowly health officials were notified.

title: Citing possible investigation, NC elections board declines to name allegedly dead voters
why: North Carolina's elections board is withholding the names of thousands of supposedly deceased people on the voter rolls, citing possible prosecutions, which keeps the public from verifying claims of fraud driving purge efforts.

title: Law enforcement didn't provide records showing immigration agreements followed state procedure, ACLU says
why: The ACLU says Wyoming sheriffs signing 287(g) deals to enforce federal immigration law failed to produce records proving they followed required state procedures, raising transparency questions as more counties deputize local police for ICE work.

title: 'Black Box' goes beneath the surface of Mississippi's opioid epidemic and settlements
why: Mississippi Today's investigation tracks how more than $400 million in opioid settlement money meant for treatment and recovery is actually being spent, scrutiny other states drawing on the same settlements will want to copy.

title: Immigrant neighbors skip mutual aid event as ICE fears increase
why: Latino families stopped showing up to a South Side food pantry after recent fatal ICE shootings, a concrete example of how immigration enforcement is cutting people off from food and basic aid in Chicago neighborhoods.

title: Hartford residents back police oversight board in union standoff
why: Community members rallied and packed a hearing to defend Hartford's civilian police review board as the police union fights to weaken it, a test case for how much power residents get over local policing.

title: ICE is arresting relatives who come forward to take custody of migrant children in federal shelters
why: Adults who step up to sponsor children held in Office of Refugee Resettlement shelters are being detained by ICE when they appear, a practice that leaves kids stuck in custody longer and deters family reunification nationwide.

title: El Paso adopts stringent rules for new data centers
why: City Council unanimously approved a framework that stops short of a ban but makes data centers far harder to permit — a concrete model for the dozens of cities from Boulder City to Jackson now fighting over water and power commitments to hyperscale campuses.

title: Officials, Neighbors Question If City Policies Aimed At Protecting Immigrants Are Being Followed
why: A City Council committee grilled Chicago police over whether they are actually honoring the mayor’s “ICE on Notice” order after officers arrested street vendors. Sanctuary policies only work if the department follows them, and this hearing tested that gap directly.

title: Children’s Hospital Colorado pleads not guilty to contempt allegation in gender-affirming care lawsuit
why: The state’s largest pediatric hospital is accused of defying a court order to resume gender-affirming care for transgender youth, with a contempt trial set for September. The ruling will set the terms for whether hospitals can withdraw care faster than courts can compel it.

title: Duke Energy Carolinas halves its rate hike request in new settlement
why: Duke cut its proposed increase to an average 3.7% over two years after regulatory pushback, directly changing the monthly bill for millions of North and South Carolina households as data-center demand drives utilities nationwide to seek higher rates.

title: Colorado River Indian Tribes reach historic agreement over water use
why: Tribes holding some of the most senior rights on the Colorado River struck a deal governing how their water can be leased and moved — a template that will shape negotiations for the 40 million people across seven states who depend on the same shrinking river.

title: Bears Ears, Grand Staircase-Escalante: Utahns protest Trump’s slashing of national monuments
why: Close to a thousand people turned out across Utah after protections were stripped from nearly three million acres, including land tribes fought for decades to safeguard. Utah’s own lawsuit against the federal government is now in limbo as a result.

title: Hinds sheriff misses judge’s deadline to release jail death records
why: A chancery judge ordered the Hinds County sheriff to hand over records on deaths inside the Raymond Detention Center by July 9; he blew the deadline. The SPLC has been seeking a full count of in-custody deaths since 2022, and 18-year-old Mielun Butler was stomped to death in the jail this month.

title: Meta wants hearing, $10K fine refunded in data center water case
why: Meta is contesting a state penalty tied to bacteria problems at its Cheyenne data center and wants the money back. It is a rare look at what happens after a tech giant is actually cited — and how small the penalty is relative to the project.

title: Immigration News Today: U.S. Seeks to Deny Green Cards to Immigrants Who Use Public Benefits
why: DHS published its final “public charge” rule on July 20, letting officers count SNAP, Medicaid and housing vouchers against green card applicants starting Sept. 18. The agency’s own estimate is that roughly 950,000 people will drop federal benefits they qualify for rather than risk their status.

title: Student loan defaults surge in Wisconsin, US after federal reprieve ends
why: More than 108,000 Wisconsinites are now in default, part of a nationwide spike since pandemic-era protections lapsed. Default triggers wage garnishment and tax-refund seizure, so the federal data analyzed here maps who is about to lose income involuntarily.

title: Curfews, Drones, and Criminal Charges: Cities Differ on Approaches to ‘Teen Takeovers’
why: Cities are answering large youth gatherings with curfews, drone surveillance and felony charges — Newport Beach alone arrested more than 400 people aged 15 to 25 over July Fourth weekend — and the reporting maps which tactics reduce harm versus which funnel teenagers into the criminal system.

title: The major takeaways from week 1 of the Sen. Jason Ellsworth criminal trial
why: Montana’s former Senate president is on trial over allegations he steered $170,100 in state contract work to a friend — one of the rare instances where a sitting legislator’s self-dealing reaches a courtroom instead of an ethics committee.

title: Laramie County sheriff ordered to appear in court, explain why law firm can’t inspect records
why: A judge is forcing a Wyoming sheriff to justify withholding records sought by attorneys in a deportation case — a direct test of whether state public-records law reaches local agencies’ cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

title: New elections rules could make ballot rejections easier in North Carolina
why: The North Carolina State Board of Elections approved rules giving officials more latitude to reject ballots beginning with the 2026 midterms — in a state whose recent statewide races have been decided by margins smaller than the number of ballots in dispute.

title: Report: Federal funding cuts drastically hurt Indigenous programs addressing domestic violence, sexual assault and MMIP
why: A new report documents how federal cuts are gutting tribal programs that shelter survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault and search for missing and murdered Indigenous people — services that in many rural tribal communities have no other provider within hours.

title: Why did energy-saving tips disappear from the Energy Department website?
why: More than 1,600 pages were deleted from the Department of Energy’s Energy Saver site by July 3, stripping out free, practical guidance that helped households cut utility bills just as electricity rates climb across much of the country.

title: L.A. saved its neediest renters. San Diego’s still waiting.
why: Los Angeles moved 4,200 formerly homeless residents onto Section 8 before pandemic-era rental aid expires; San Diego housing officials still have no plan, leaving thousands of people at risk of returning to the street this fall.

title: WVU Health knew about painkiller theft. They failed to deal with it for years.
why: West Virginia’s largest hospital system agreed to a $4.1 million federal settlement after failing for years to report or stop employees stealing opioids and other addictive drugs — drug diversion inside the health system serving the state hit hardest by the overdose crisis.

title: DCF data reveals new details about child deaths
why: Newly released state data details 28 deaths — by suicide, homicide, accident and medical cause — of Connecticut children whose families had open or recently closed child-protective cases since January 2025, the kind of case-level accounting most states still decline to publish.

title: Texas paid investigators to probe Islamic private schools applying to its voucher program
why: Texas spent taxpayer money contracting investigators — one of them convicted of libel in Britain — to dig into nearly 50 private schools over alleged ties to radical Islamic organizations and the Chinese government, as the state decides which schools receive public voucher dollars.

title: Ghost gun company ordered to pay $104 million in Kentucky case, ‘largest in U.S. history’
why: A Louisville jury ordered a ghost-gun kit maker to pay $104 million to the mother of a shooting victim — the largest verdict ever against a gun dealer in the U.S. — a ruling that could expose the online untraceable-firearms industry to a wave of liability suits nationwide.

title: Wildfire smoke brings hazardous air quality in Wisconsin. Here’s how to stay safe
why: Smoke from Canadian and Minnesota wildfires pushed air quality across Wisconsin and the Upper Midwest into ‘hazardous’ territory — some of the worst on record — forcing school and pool closures and underscoring how cross-border wildfire seasons are becoming a routine public-health emergency.

title: Mexico asks U.S. state attorneys general to investigate migrant deaths in ICE custody
why: Mexico is formally asking U.S. state attorneys general to open criminal investigations into the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals in ICE custody or enforcement operations since Trump’s second term began — a rare cross-border escalation over detention conditions and the Houston killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.

title: Trump administration revives rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits
why: The Trump administration is reviving the ‘public charge’ rule, which could deny green cards to immigrants who use benefits like Medicaid, food stamps or housing vouchers — a change that could force millions of mixed-status families to choose between aid and legal residency.

title: Feeding Our Future suspect back in U.S. after four years on the run
why: Abdikerm Eidleh, a key defendant in the roughly $250 million Feeding Our Future pandemic food-aid scheme — the largest COVID-relief fraud in the country — has been extradited from Somalia after four years on the run, reviving accountability in a case that has already convicted dozens in Minnesota.

title: Lawsuit blames southern Colorado electric company for starting, spreading Aspen Acres fire
why: A new lawsuit blames San Isabel Electric Association’s power lines for igniting and spreading the Aspen Acres fire — now the seventh-largest in Colorado history at nearly 100,000 acres and 850 destroyed structures — reviving the fight over utility responsibility for catastrophic Western wildfires.

title: One of Utah’s biggest environmental cleanups is nearly finished
why: Utah is nearing the end of one of the country’s largest environmental cleanups, having hauled away 16 million tons of Cold War–era uranium tailings from the banks of the Colorado River near Moab — removing a decades-old contamination threat to a water source for 40 million people downstream.

title: Google is building a $500 million data center in rural Ohio. Neighbors are furious
why: Google is building a $500 million data center on 373 acres of former farmland near Lima, and residents of the 14,500-person township are furious over water use, noise and tax breaks — a local flashpoint in the national fight over the AI boom’s rural footprint.

title: Chicago Police Promised To ‘Fix’ Secret Traffic Stops. A Year Later, The Problem Has Only Gotten Worse
why: A year after Chicago police vowed to fix a system of ‘secret’ traffic stops that officers weren’t reporting to oversight agencies as state law requires, Block Club found the problem has grown worse — leaving a racially lopsided stop program running with almost no accountability.

title: She Abused a Minor. He Served Time for Rape. They Both Launched Private Schools Taking Public Money.
why: A Mountain State Spotlight–ProPublica investigation found that a Florida teacher who lost her license for sexually abusing a 16-year-old, and a man who served prison time for rape, each opened private schools now collecting taxpayer-funded voucher money — exposing how little vetting the fast-growing school-choice programs require.

title: After week of silence, Gov. Greg Abbott calls fatal ICE shooting “tragic”
why: After a week of silence, Gov. Greg Abbott called the ICE killing of Houston-area resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo “tragic” and confirmed Texas DPS and the Rangers will investigate — the first state accountability step after federal agents shot a man they later admitted was not their target.

title: Eastern Kentucky judge orders Jim Justice coal company to pay millions in lawsuit
why: A federal judge ordered a coal company tied to U.S. Sen. Jim Justice to pay more than $18 million, escalating penalties in a decade-long case and putting fresh legal pressure on the finances of a sitting senator’s family business.

title: Ben & Jerry’s Foundation says it will shut down amid legal dispute with parent company
why: The Ben & Jerry’s Foundation will close after parent company Unilever cut its funding and evicted its staff, ending $600,000 a year in Vermont grants and 40 years of the brand’s progressive giving as the two sides fight in court.

title: Trump’s shrinking of Utah monuments leaves state’s lawsuit against federal government in limbo. Here’s why.
why: Trump’s order shrinking Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante strips protection from millions of acres and throws Utah’s own lawsuit over the monuments into limbo, reshaping the long fight over control of Western public lands.

title: Report: ICE detainees at Camp East Montana report frequent beatings and other human rights abuses
why: An 84-page Human Rights Watch and ACLU report documents detainees at the Fort Bliss “Camp East Montana” tent facility being beaten by guards, denied medical care and fed inedible food — the first detailed account of conditions inside one of the largest new ICE detention sites in the country.

title: Cleveland to keep Flock cameras, pause new data center projects
why: Cleveland’s City Council voted 9-6 to keep its 100 Flock license-plate-reader cameras for another six months while pausing new data center projects — a decision at the center of a national debate over mass surveillance and Big Tech’s local footprint.

title: Authorities in Campbell County transferred 87 people to ICE custody in 13-month period
why: Local law enforcement in a single Wyoming county funneled 87 people into ICE custody over 13 months — a rare hard count showing how deeply routine county policing now feeds the federal deportation machine in rural America.

title: ICE Hasn’t Reported Detention or Deportation Data in Months
why: ICE has stopped publishing the detention and deportation figures it released for years, leaving the public, courts and Congress with no official count of who the agency is holding or removing during its largest enforcement surge in decades.

title: Investigation into possible tuberculosis spread at Aurora ICE facility blocked by private company, health officials say
why: GEO Group, which runs the Aurora immigration detention center, is blocking county health officials from investigating a possible tuberculosis outbreak inside — raising the risk that a highly contagious disease spreads unchecked among detainees and staff.

title: They wanted to hold Exxon accountable. Then they got hacked.
why: Environmental lawyers and activists preparing climate-liability cases against ExxonMobil were targeted by a hacking operation that stole their emails and surfaced them in court — a case that could chill accountability litigation against fossil fuel companies nationwide.

title: Work at South County ICE facility temporarily paused
why: Under a court agreement in Santa Clara County and California's lawsuit, Homeland Security paused construction on a South County ICE detention site until Sept. 9 — a temporary win for local officials trying to block new federal detention capacity in a self-declared sanctuary county.

title: DCF moves to dismiss victim’s claim in Waterbury captivity case
why: Connecticut's child-welfare agency is asking a court to throw out a lawsuit from a man who says he was held captive by his stepmother for two decades, arguing it can't be sued for failing to act on abuse reports it received between 1996 and 2005 — a test of whether the state can be held liable for missed warnings.

title: Gov. Reeves calls special session
why: Gov. Tate Reeves summoned Mississippi lawmakers back to the Capitol for a special session, forcing action on unfinished state business and setting up a high-stakes fight over spending priorities in one of the nation's poorest states.

title: Montana’s Republican loyalty battle gets a hearing in court
why: New Montana GOP rules demand loyalty oaths and threaten to punish elected officials — potentially even the governor — who defy party leaders, a clash now before a judge that could test whether a party can override the state constitution to discipline officeholders.

title: Do no ‘harm’: Feds rescind ESA definition protecting habitat
why: The Interior Department formally dropped “harm” — long read to include habitat destruction — from what the Endangered Species Act prohibits, a change that weakens protections for imperiled species nationwide and clears the way for development on sensitive lands.

title: ICE to scale back traffic stops as Charlotte sees recent increase in arrests
why: The Trump administration has ordered ICE to largely stop routine traffic stops nationwide after two fatal shootings — a policy shift that reaches Charlotte just as vehicle stops and arrests there were climbing, and that will reshape enforcement in cities across the country.

title: Hilleary and Garrett lead Tennessee District 6 race
why: Van Hilleary and Johnny Garrett have emerged as front-runners in the crowded GOP primary to succeed Rep. John Rose in Tennessee's 6th District, a race centered on affordability and ‘America First’ themes that will shape the seat for a solidly Republican region.

title: The US may be hitting a tipping point for heat pumps
why: Heat pump sales have doubled in 15 years and, in early 2026, outpaced gas furnace shipments by 32% — a shift that could cut household emissions and energy bills nationwide even as federal policy swings toward fossil fuels.

title: Federal Prisoners Give Advice on How to Fix the Grievance Process
why: With fewer than 2% of federal prison grievances granted in 2023, incarcerated people describe how the Bureau of Prisons' paperwork maze buries complaints about everything from healthcare to book bans — and often blocks prisoners from ever suing over conditions.

title: Jefferson County Clerk picked friend, donor and business partner to oversee elections, IT
why: Three weeks into the job, new Jefferson County Clerk David Yates gave a no-bid, $3,000-a-week consulting contract to the mother of his friend and business partner — putting a political ally in charge of election administration and IT for one of Kentucky's largest counties.

title: A 'crisis communication gap' threatens Indigenous peoples
why: A wildfire that forced the Xeni Gwet'in First Nation to evacuate exposed a dangerous gap in emergency alert systems for Indigenous communities — a breakdown that mirrors risks facing tribal nations across North America as climate disasters intensify.

title: Two JCPS school board candidates filed in wrong districts
why: Two candidates for the Jefferson County school board filed to run in districts where they don't live, an eligibility problem LPM uncovered that could disqualify contenders for a body overseeing one of Kentucky's largest school systems.

title: Work at South County ICE facility temporarily paused
why: Construction on a planned ICE detention facility in South Santa Clara County was temporarily halted — a reprieve for immigrant-rights advocates fighting to keep new federal detention capacity out of a county that calls itself a sanctuary.

title: NC state employees get another premium hike, but health insurance changes could lower other costs
why: More than 77,000 North Carolina state employees will pay higher health premiums for the second straight year as the State Health Plan works to close a projected $1 billion deficit for 2027, squeezing teachers and public workers already stretched by rising costs.

title: Teen killer of Dartmouth professors in 2001 resentenced, eligible for parole in 20 years
why: Robert Tulloch, who murdered two Dartmouth professors in 2001 as a teenager, was resentenced and could be paroled by age 62 — the latest application of court rulings barring mandatory life-without-parole for juveniles that is reshaping decades-old cases nationwide.

title: Feds share evidence in Good, Pretti shootings with state investigators months after stonewalling
why: Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced federal authorities finally handed over evidence in the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti — months after the Trump administration tried to lock state investigators out — reviving the prospect of state charges against the federal agents involved.

title: $31.5 million for uninsured Kansas Citians goes to the same six providers
why: More than two months behind schedule, Kansas City approved $31.5 million to care for uninsured residents — but all of it flowed to the same six providers the health levy has funded for years, concentrating the region's safety net in a handful of organizations.

title: Mississippi is getting hotter. Experts say it's hurting moms and babies
why: Extreme heat raises the risk of preterm birth and stillbirth, and Mississippi — with long, muggy summers and many families who can't afford air conditioning — is especially exposed, endangering pregnant women and infants in one of the nation's poorest states.

title: Jackson bus drivers go on strike after latest contract impasse with MV Transportation
why: Jackson transit workers walked off the job Monday after weekend contract talks with MV Transportation collapsed, stranding riders who depend on JTRAN buses in a capital city where many residents have no other way to reach work, groceries or medical care.

title: No federal heat standard? NYC workers are building their own safety net
why: With no federal heat-safety rule for workers, New York City labor groups are training their own members — like UPS drivers — to survive dangerous on-the-job heat, a do-it-yourself model other cities may copy as extreme heat becomes routine.

title: How federal prison guards stop lawsuits before they start
why: A Marshall Project and NPR investigation found fewer than 2% of grievances filed in federal prison in 2023 were granted, and prisoners who complain about mistreatment routinely face retaliation — keeping abuse hidden and blocking lawsuits before they can be filed.

title: As a strong El Niño develops off the Pacific, experts say Vermont impact is tough to tease out
why: A strengthening El Niño is reshaping global weather, but forecasters caution Vermonters — in a state scarred by repeat July floods — that its local effects remain hard to predict even as odds tilt toward a hotter summer.

title: Pennsylvania poised to adopt $50.8B budget that sends more money to poorest schools
why: Nearly two weeks late, PA lawmakers advanced a $50.8B budget directing more than $900M to the poorest schools and requiring data centers to disclose energy and water use — while punting on regulating newly-illegal skill games.

title: A county's struggle to pass a school levy exposes gaps in West Virginia's education funding
why: Summers County's repeated levy failures — leaving staffing cuts and crumbling buildings — show how West Virginia's funding formula pushes poor, rural districts to lean on local property taxes their residents can't afford.

title: Hundreds in Houston protest ICE killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo
why: Surveillance video and passenger accounts contradict ICE's claim that Salgado Araujo tried to ram agents with his van, as protesters demand release of footage — a flashpoint in mounting scrutiny of immigration agents who wore no body cameras.

title: The oceans are full of heat, and it's coming ashore
why: Nearly 40% of the world's ocean is in a marine heatwave, with Mediterranean and Pacific waters more than 10°F above normal — fueling record land heat that killed dozens over the holiday weekend and threatening fisheries and coral worldwide.

title: With the white nationalist group Patriot Front, what you see is not what you get
why: After hundreds of masked Patriot Front members marched through Washington over July Fourth weekend, WFAE unpacks how the group's uniformed, sanitized image masks a violent white-nationalist agenda organizing across the country.

title: East San Jose charter school allowed to stay open — for now
why: A judge ordered the district to keep Escuela Popular — a bilingual school serving immigrant families — open after finding officials used the wrong legal standard to revoke its charter, a reprieve for hundreds of students weeks before a planned closure.

title: More CT residents are taking testosterone
why: Androgen prescriptions in Connecticut jumped 63% in three years, a surge that outpaces clear medical guidance and raises questions about the aggressive marketing of hormone therapy to men.

title: Victor Marx wins Colorado’s three-way Republican primary for governor
why: More than a week after polls closed, first-time candidate Victor Marx edged state Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer to win the GOP nomination, giving Republicans a long-shot chance to end 20 years of Democratic control of the governor’s office.

title: Kentucky congressman ‘absolutely opposed’ to in-state hyperscale data centers
why: Rep. Morgan McGarvey told a packed Louisville crowd he opposes a proposed 400-megawatt data center in west Louisville, adding a federal voice to a fast-spreading local backlash over the power and water these facilities consume.

title: Teen stomped to death in Hinds jail, coroner says
why: A 19-year-old held on a $1 million bond was stomped to death inside the Hinds County jail within a day of being booked, the coroner says, spotlighting deadly violence and thin supervision in a Mississippi lockup already under federal scrutiny.

title: Appeals court ends Texas in-state tuition for undocumented students
why: A federal appeals court let stand a ruling ending the Texas Dream Act, stripping in-state tuition from undocumented students who have lived in Texas for years and pricing many out of public college overnight.

title: New filing in border patrol agent’s killing challenges law enforcement version of events
why: Lawyers for Teresa Youngblut, charged in the fatal shooting of Border Patrol Agent David Maland, say evidence contradicts the federal account of what triggered the deadly Vermont traffic stop — raising doubts in one of the year’s highest-profile immigration-enforcement killings.

title: Billionaire makes huge contribution to political group backing Ohio GOP candidate Vivek Ramaswamy
why: Billionaire Jeff Yass gave $10 million to a PAC backing Vivek Ramaswamy’s run for Ohio governor, an early sign of how much out-of-state money will flood one of 2026’s marquee governor’s races.

title: ICE is building a ‘hard-sided’ detention facility near Buffalo. What does that mean?
why: ICE is adding 100 beds to New York’s only agency-run detention center in Batavia but won’t say what the expansion will look like, as it races to replace jail space it will lose under a new state law barring county-jail detention.

title: New Utah monument will include an Indigenous man with a tomahawk. Native nations see it as a stereotype.
why: A planned Salt Lake City monument depicts a tomahawk-wielding Native man clashing with a settler, and tribal nations say it revives a demeaning ‘savage’ stereotype — reigniting a national argument over how public art portrays Indigenous people.

title: Yale community mobilizes against reported Justice Dept. settlement
why: Yale faculty and students are organizing against a reported federal settlement over claims the medical school kept weighing race in admissions after the 2023 Supreme Court ban — a fight that could set the terms for how Washington polices affirmative action at elite universities.

title: Can Republicans undistrict Montana’s Native vote?
why: After the U.S. Supreme Court struck down race-based redistricting, Montana Republicans are moving to dismantle legislative districts drawn to give Native American voters representation — an early test of a strategy that could erase minority-opportunity districts across the country.

title: Vigil for Houston man killed by ICE draws crowd as Rep. Al Green vows impeachment articles
why: Hundreds gathered in Houston to mourn Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, killed in an ICE operation, as U.S. Rep. Al Green announced he will file articles of impeachment against President Trump over immigration enforcement — turning a local death into a national confrontation.

title: Minneapolis police drone plan for 911 calls sparks privacy concerns
why: Nearly 50 residents packed a Minneapolis council meeting to oppose a plan letting police send Skydio drones to 911 calls before officers arrive, raising surveillance and civil-liberties fears — part of a growing national debate over drones as first responders.

title: Phil Scott issues executive order that would allow age-based health insurance premiums
why: Gov. Phil Scott's executive order would let insurers charge older Vermonters higher premiums in a bid to lower costs for younger enrollees, a deregulation move that could shift health-cost burdens onto those most likely to need care.

title: Former Wisconsin judge Hannah Dugan spared prison for obstructing ICE arrest
why: A federal judge fined former Milwaukee judge Hannah Dugan $5,000 but spared her prison for ushering a defendant out of her courtroom to evade ICE, a closely watched test of how far judges can go to resist federal immigration enforcement.

title: Trump pardons Hendersonville mechanic convicted of violating the Clean Air Act
why: President Trump pardoned a North Carolina mechanic and 10 others convicted mostly of Clean Air Act violations, signaling leniency toward the emissions-cheating cases that environmental prosecutors spent years building.

title: Federal judge orders immediate release of Bozeman resident from immigration detention
why: A federal judge ruled ICE violated a 20-year-old Bozeman resident's due-process rights by jailing him without a bond hearing and ordered his immediate release, echoing a broader legal fight over 'mandatory detention' now playing out in courts nationwide.

title: Metro Council advances data center zoning bills after marathon public hearing
why: More than 100 residents testified against data center development as Metro Council advanced zoning rules for the power-hungry facilities, part of a wave of local pushback as data centers strain electricity grids from Tennessee to Ohio.

title: Detroit asylum approval rate plummets to 2% — lowest in at least 25 years
why: Approval rates for Detroit asylum seekers have collapsed to just 2% of cases in 2026 — the lowest in at least 25 years — meaning almost everyone who files a claim is now denied, a shift that reshapes the odds for thousands fleeing persecution.

title: Pfizer building subcontractor had years of safety warnings before near-collapse
why: A labor union warned for three years about a demolition subcontractor's safety record before a former Pfizer building in Manhattan nearly collapsed, exposing how thin oversight of contractors can put workers and the public at risk.

title: Supreme Court will hear Nebraska's fight over access to Colorado's South Platte River
why: The U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear Nebraska's bid to build a canal diverting water from Colorado's South Platte River, a case that could redraw water rights across the drought-stressed West as states fight over a shrinking supply.

title: Babylon Fire surpasses 100,000 acres, remains 0% contained
why: Utah's Babylon Fire has grown past 100,000 acres with zero containment and more than 1,200 personnel assigned, making it the largest active wildfire in the country as crews fight to protect homes around Monticello.

title: Aspen Acres fire grows to nearly 94,000 acres as forecasters eye chance of rain
why: Colorado's Aspen Acres fire has burned nearly 94,000 acres and destroyed at least 263 homes, and firefighters are pinning hopes on incoming monsoon rains for the first real containment help since the blaze ignited June 29.

title: Wisconsin Supreme Court rejects 2020 election investigator's attempt to get voting eligibility records
why: A 5-2 Wisconsin Supreme Court ruling shielded records about people deemed mentally incompetent to vote from a 2020 election investigator, with a conservative justice joining liberals to keep sensitive voter data out of public-records reach ahead of the midterms.

title: DeSoto County residents file lawsuit over majority-Black judicial subdistrict
why: DeSoto County residents, including a former GOP gubernatorial candidate, sued to overturn Mississippi's new majority-Black judicial subdistricts, arguing the Legislature's map violates the Voting Rights Act — a case that could reshape how judges are elected across the South.

title: Data centers drive up electricity costs for Tennessee residents
why: A new Think Tennessee report finds residents in areas hosting data centers foot a disproportionate share of rising electricity bills, quantifying a cost shift as the energy-hungry facilities multiply — a fight also playing out in Ohio, Indiana, Wisconsin and beyond.

title: New lawsuit alleges U.S. shared asylum application details with Iran
why: A federal lawsuit alleges U.S. officials handed Iranian asylum seekers' application details to Tehran — the very government they fled — a breach that could expose applicants and their families to imprisonment or worse and calls the confidentiality of the entire asylum system into question.

title: Caution grips Gallatin Co. Latino community after immigration enforcement operations
why: Immigration raids have left many in Gallatin County's Latino community afraid to leave home, prompting nonprofits to deliver groceries and supplies — a window into how aggressive enforcement is reshaping daily life in rural Western communities.

title: Kentucky awarded $1.3B of single-bid asphalt contracts in past 3 years, report shows
why: A think-tank review found Kentucky's transportation cabinet awarded $1.3 billion in road-paving contracts over three years that drew only a single bidder, raising questions about whether taxpayers overpay when competition disappears — a procurement pattern many states share.

title: Planned Parenthood regains federal funding as 1-year freeze ends
why: Planned Parenthood regained access to federal Medicaid reimbursement for non-abortion services after a one-year funding freeze expired, restoring a revenue stream that affects clinics and low-income patients in many states.

title: Pritzker signs landmark AI regulation bill that aims to mitigate risks
why: Illinois became one of the first states to enact broad AI safeguards, requiring companies to test high-risk systems for bias and discrimination — a template statehouses nationwide are watching closely as federal AI rules stall.

title: Aspen Acres destruction climbs to 263 homes lost in Pueblo, Custer counties
why: The Aspen Acres fire has now destroyed 263 homes and four commercial buildings and sits at just 13% containment, making it one of Colorado's most destructive blazes this year as crews battle multiple fires that have scorched well over 90,000 acres.

title: Court blocks Trump administration changes to homelessness funding
why: A federal court sided with Connecticut and 19 other states plus D.C. to block HUD's rollback of Continuum of Care grants, preserving more than $3 billion nationally and keeping housing and mental-health services flowing to roughly 170,000 people.

title: The system built to prevent massive floods in Chicago near capacity after 'stunning' rainfall
why: Chicago's Deep Tunnel reservoirs are nearly full after near-record early-summer rain - McCook has already hit capacity six times this year - testing the region's multibillion-dollar flood defenses as climate-driven downpours intensify.

title: Proposed oil pipeline to British Columbia coast spurs alarm in Washington state
why: Alberta's route for a 1-million-barrel-a-day crude pipeline ends about a mile from Washington waters, and tribes and environmental groups warn the added tanker traffic threatens endangered orcas and raises spill risk across the shared Salish Sea.

title: Former Jackson Mayor Lumumba and ex-council member Banks plead guilty in public corruption case
why: Former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba and ex-councilman Aaron Banks pleaded guilty to federal conspiracy charges tied to a bribery, wire-fraud and money-laundering scheme, capping a years-long FBI probe that upends leadership in Mississippi's largest and majority-Black capital city.

title: NC lawmakers finally agreed on a budget. Here's what it means for you
why: North Carolina's General Assembly passed its first comprehensive spending plan in more than two years, ending a lengthy stalemate and setting funding for schools, raises and services that shape daily life for 10 million residents.

title: US Supreme Court ruling on deportation protections leaves Vermont Haitians out of work and scrambling for options
why: The Supreme Court's June decision letting the administration end Temporary Protected Status has already cost dozens of Haitian workers their jobs across Vermont industries, a local jolt from a national ruling affecting hundreds of thousands of TPS holders.

title: In Mississippi, summer can increase risk of hunger for 3 in 4 kids who rely on in-school meals
why: Gov. Tate Reeves again declined the federal SUN Bucks summer grocery program, turning down about $38 million that would have fed roughly 320,000 low-income Mississippi children - a decision other GOP-led states are weighing that leaves families to cover the gap.

title: How inconsistent standards led to dozens of disenfranchised voters in Mequon
why: Mequon clerks applied an unusually strict reading of witness-address rules and rejected dozens of absentee ballots, exposing how uneven local standards can quietly disenfranchise voters - a warning for battleground states heading into the 2026 midterms.

title: Fast-tracked immigration hearings leave migrant children facing deportation alone, without lawyers
why: A 7-year-old asked a judge to reunite him with his deported father during a 10-minute hearing - one of a wave of unaccompanied children pushed through accelerated proceedings without attorneys as the Trump administration speeds removals, a due-process shift with national reach.

title: Bolstered bloc of Vermont Republicans see bills repealed this year as a win
why: Vermont’s enlarged Republican minority is claiming victory this session not for laws it passed but for measures it rolled back, a shift that signals growing GOP leverage in a state long dominated by Democrats.

title: China resumes US soybean purchases under trade deal with Trump, but future for farmers remains ‘daunting’
why: China — the biggest buyer of American soybeans — is placing orders again after a new trade deal, but volumes remain far below pre-trade-war levels, leaving Mississippi and Midwest growers financially exposed heading into harvest.

title: Aspen Acres fire grows to 87,000 acres as firefighting force expands on Fourth of July holiday
why: The Aspen Acres fire nearly doubled to about 87,000 acres over the holiday — one of five major Colorado wildfires burning nearly 180,000 acres combined — as crews expanded and officials urged residents to skip fireworks amid widening evacuations.

title: This summer’s ‘dead zone’ in the Gulf will be larger than average
why: NOAA forecasts a low-oxygen ‘dead zone’ topping 7,000 square miles this summer, driven by Mississippi River nutrient pollution that suffocates marine life and squeezes fisheries across the Gulf Coast.

title: ‘A self-inflicted tragedy’: Congress approves reversal of US climate policy
why: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act — signed into law July 4 — sunsets the Inflation Reduction Act’s clean-energy tax credits, gutting the only federal climate strategy and stranding wind and solar projects nationwide unless they break ground within days.

title: ‘This is My Country Now’: 52 new citizens naturalized on Long Island before July 4
why: At a Long Island ceremony, 52 immigrants became U.S. citizens just before July 4 — a snapshot of the naturalization path continuing even as the Supreme Court’s TPS ruling and stepped-up enforcement unsettle immigrant communities.

title: The days are hot, but so are the nights. That’s a problem, experts say
why: As a heat dome bakes up to 90 million Americans, LPM examines how rising overnight temperatures rob bodies of recovery time — a mounting public-health risk that makes heat waves deadlier, especially for people without air conditioning.

title: State budget revisions save Santa Clara County from deeper cuts
why: California’s newly signed budget delivers $900 million for homeless services — nearly double Gov. Newsom’s proposal — while preserving in-home care and mobile mental-health teams and delaying some Medi-Cal cuts for immigrants, sparing Santa Clara County from the deepest reductions.

title: What, to the Immigrant, Is Your Fourth of July?
why: On the nation’s 250th birthday, currently and formerly detained immigrants describe what citizenship and belonging mean amid intensified ICE enforcement — first-person reporting that reframes the holiday from inside the immigration system.

title: Texas Stock Exchange to launch trading Monday
why: Backed by BlackRock and Citadel Securities, the Dallas-based Texas Stock Exchange begins a phased launch this week — the best-funded challenge to the NYSE–Nasdaq duopoly in decades, with major stocks set to trade by month’s end.

title: Colorado’s wildfires scorch 129,000 acres as critical fire danger persists
why: Six large wildfires have burned more than 200 square miles across Colorado, with the Aspen Acres fire alone destroying as many as 200 structures and forcing widening evacuations as hot, dry, windy weather offers little relief.

title: Appeals court says undocumented immigrants must get bond hearings
why: The 5th Circuit ruled the government can’t detain undocumented immigrants indefinitely without a bond hearing, rejecting a Trump administration policy and potentially affecting thousands held in detention across Texas and beyond.

title: 5 people sue Border Patrol agents over use of tear gas, unlawful detention during Midway Blitz
why: Five Chicagoans allege Border Patrol agents tear-gassed and unlawfully detained them during an immigration operation on the Southwest Side — among the first lawsuits to challenge the tactics used in the city’s “Midway Blitz” enforcement surge.

title: Senatobia police stonewall requests for details of officer shooting that killed 1-year-old outside Walmart
why: Weeks after an officer shot and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley during a shoplifting call, Senatobia police are withholding basic records about the shooting, testing Mississippi’s public-records law amid mounting demands for accountability.

title: State budget will defund IOLTA, leaving many poor North Carolinians without civil legal support
why: North Carolina’s budget strips funding from the account that bankrolls civil legal aid, threatening representation for the state’s poorest residents in eviction, domestic-violence and benefits cases — a cut other states could copy.

title: Workforce Pell is here. States are racing to catch up.
why: A new federal program lets low-income students use Pell grants for short-term job training for the first time, but uneven state readiness means many of the roughly 100,000 students expected to benefit each year won’t see aid for months or years.

title: NY budget lets Hochul spend $1.5B without normal oversight
why: Lawmakers quietly exempted nearly $1.5 billion from the state comptroller’s contract review in the new budget, letting Gov. Hochul’s administration sign deals without the watchdog scrutiny normally required — a rollback of a key anti-corruption check.

title: Danger Behind Bars: Mississippi keeps sending suicidal prisoners to solitary
why: Nearly 50 people have died by suicide in Mississippi’s solitary-confinement units since 2015, yet the state keeps isolating vulnerable prisoners despite evidence the practice deepens mental illness — a joint investigation with Mississippi Today and the Clarion Ledger.

title: UPS didn’t require inspection of part that failed before deadly Louisville crash
why: UPS never required the detailed inspections that could have caught the engine-mount failure blamed for a crash that killed 15 people last fall — raising hard questions about maintenance oversight at one of the nation’s largest air-cargo carriers.

title: Congressional Black Caucus hit by Supreme Court ruling
why: A Supreme Court decision weakening the tools used to draw majority-Black districts threatens the political clout of the Congressional Black Caucus, with ripple effects for minority representation in Connecticut and states nationwide.

title: ‘This has become a national fight’: Aspen Acres fire expands, scorching 35,000 acres
why: The wind-driven Aspen Acres fire has burned 35,000 acres and destroyed more than 180 structures across Pueblo and Custer counties, forcing an out-of-state incident team to take command as evacuations widen.

title: Officer who shot baby Kohen Wiley in Senatobia was not in harm’s way, family attorney says
why: An independent autopsy presented by attorney Ben Crump contradicts the police account of a Senatobia officer who shot and killed a 1-year-old, intensifying scrutiny of the shooting and demands for accountability.

title: La Tuna federal prison in Anthony to close, ending nearly a century of operations
why: The Bureau of Prisons will shutter the 94-year-old La Tuna complex, eliminating hundreds of local jobs as part of a nationwide closure push driven by aging infrastructure and staffing shortages.

title: New Britain to sue Erin Stewart after missed repayment deadline
why: New Britain’s mayor is suing his predecessor, former mayor Erin Stewart, to recover more than $100,000 tied to how she improperly boosted her own pay over 12 years — a notable municipal accountability case.

title: Days After Supreme Court TPS Ruling, Little Haiti Wonders What’s Next
why: After the Supreme Court cleared the way for the administration to end Temporary Protected Status, roughly 330,000 Haitians nationwide face deportation; Documented captures the fear gripping Brooklyn’s Little Haiti.

title: DeKalb Rejects Data Center Regulations, but Fight Continues
why: DeKalb County commissioners voted down proposed data center rules after a year of resident pushback, a decision that tests how majority-Black communities can shape the fast-growing industry reshaping neighborhoods nationwide.

title: As Montana’s Medicaid work requirements loom, questions about system gaps remain
why: Montana is among the first states to impose Medicaid work requirements, and reporting reveals unresolved system gaps that could cost eligible low-income residents their coverage — a preview for the many states following suit.

title: On the upper Texas coast, many petrochemical facilities may not be prepared for fiercer storms
why: A Tribune investigation finds many Gulf Coast petrochemical plants — sources of toxic releases during past hurricanes — remain underprepared for stronger storms, exposing nearby communities to chemical hazards as climate-driven weather intensifies.

title: Jefferson County Clerk, state elections officials offer dueling takes on ballot errors
why: Following an LPM investigation into misassigned ballots, the county clerk and state officials clash over blame, and the clerk now seeks funding to audit precinct assignments for nearly 600,000 addresses before the next election.

title: DACA Recipients Detained, Deported by Trump Administration
why: The Trump administration has begun detaining and deporting DACA recipients despite polling showing broad public support for protecting them — a major escalation that puts roughly 500,000 “Dreamers” at risk of removal.

title: Phil Weiser beats U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet in Colorado’s Democratic primary for governor
why: Attorney General Phil Weiser knocked off sitting U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet in the governor’s primary, and 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros ousted longtime Rep. Diana DeGette — a night of insurgent upsets that signals how far the party’s energy has shifted from its establishment.

title: Utah’s massive Cottonwood Fire has already destroyed more than 100 structures, cost over $20M
why: The wind-driven Cottonwood Fire has leveled more than 100 structures and run up a $20 million firefighting bill, with families waiting days to learn whether their cabins survived — the latest sign of how a drought-stricken West is entering an explosive and costly fire season.

title: Order restored after hours-long hostage standoff inside ENC regional detention center
why: An hours-long hostage standoff at the Bertie-Martin Regional Detention Center in Windsor exposed the volatility inside a rural North Carolina jail that also holds immigration detainees, raising fresh questions about staffing and conditions at facilities far from public view.

title: 25 states sue Trump administration over Medicaid work requirements
why: Connecticut joined 24 other states and D.C. in suing to block new federal Medicaid work rules that health officials warn could strip coverage from hundreds of thousands of low-income adults — a fight whose outcome will decide who keeps their health insurance in dozens of states.

title: San Marcos becomes the first Texas city to ban data centers, testing its local control
why: San Marcos banned data centers within city limits, becoming a test case for whether local governments can keep the power-and-water-hungry facilities out — the same fight now playing out in West Virginia, Nashville, Kansas City and rural communities across the country.

title: Nearly 27,000 Mississippi college students may see state support shrink as aid programs face a shortfall
why: A funding shortfall in Mississippi’s financial aid programs could shrink grants for almost 27,000 students, and lawmakers say a fix may not come until 2027 — leaving low-income students in one of the nation’s poorest states uncertain whether they can afford to return in the fall.

title: U.S. Supreme Court rejects Trump’s attempt to end birthright citizenship
why: On the final day of its term the Supreme Court, 6-3, upheld the 14th Amendment’s guarantee of citizenship for nearly all children born on U.S. soil, firmly rejecting Trump’s day-one executive order — a ruling that settles the status of millions of U.S.-born children of immigrants nationwide.

title: Who were the Midway Blitz Border Patrol agents? Most were veteran immigration officers
why: Block Club identified the Border Patrol agents who carried out Chicago’s aggressive “Midway Blitz” immigration sweeps, finding most were seasoned officers reassigned from the border — a rare look at who is actually conducting the interior raids reshaping immigrant neighborhoods.

title: Why is it so unusually expensive to replace lead pipes in Chicago?
why: Chicago says replacing each of its 400,000-plus lead service lines — the nation’s largest inventory — costs about $31,000, more than six times the EPA’s $4,700 national estimate, a cost gap that threatens to leave the poorest residents drinking from lead pipes long after federal deadlines pass.

title: Digging In: What happened as Louisville jail’s healthcare provider went bankrupt
why: An investigation traces how the private company paid to provide medical care inside Louisville’s jail slid into bankruptcy, leaving incarcerated people with gaps in treatment — a cautionary tale for the many jails that outsource inmate health care to for-profit vendors.

title: Tameshia Shelton freed after 11 years as appeals court finds her guilt was never proven
why: An appeals court freed Tameshia Shelton on her birthday after 11 years in prison, ruling prosecutors never proved her guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in a 2015 murder case — a wrongful-conviction reversal that spotlights how thin evidence can still send people to prison for life.

title: Ruling blocking Trump's SAVE system won't help Texas voters already flagged as noncitizens
why: A court blocked the Trump administration's use of the federal SAVE database to flag noncitizen voters, but Texans already wrongly marked for removal get no automatic relief — leaving thousands to prove their citizenship before they can cast a ballot.

title: Florida's 'Alligator Alcatraz' immigration detention center has closed, governor says
why: Florida's governor says the Everglades detention camp that became a national symbol of harsh immigration enforcement has closed and its detainees moved elsewhere, a reversal that reshapes scrutiny of the conditions migrants endured there.

title: Hinds County DA Jody Owens pleads guilty to federal conspiracy charge, will resign
why: The district attorney for Mississippi's largest county admitted to a federal conspiracy charge from an FBI public-corruption sting and will resign Wednesday, a stunning fall for Jackson's top prosecutor that upends who oversees criminal justice in the state capital.

title: Weekend flooding highlights persistent problems with Kentucky dam safety
why: Weekend flooding exposed how many of Kentucky's aging dams are privately owned and lack money for repairs or emergency plans, leaving downstream communities at risk as extreme rainfall grows more frequent.

title: ICE ramps up operations in Milwaukee while advocates rush to catch up
why: ICE arrested dozens of people across greater Milwaukee in a weekend 'targeted operation,' leaving immigrant families and legal advocates scrambling to locate detainees — part of an enforcement surge hitting Midwestern cities far from the southern border.

title: Officials identify three federal firefighters killed battling wind-driven Snyder Fire
why: Federal officials named the three Rifle Helitack crew members — two of them women in their 20s — killed as 100-mph winds drove the Snyder Fire across the Colorado-Utah line, underscoring the deadly conditions facing wildland crews as an explosive fire season grips the drought-stricken West.

title: One year later, Ohio professors say Senate Bill 1 changed how they teach and work
why: A year after Ohio's Senate Bill 1 banned most campus DEI work and stripped faculty strike rights, professors describe canceled programs, new civics mandates and self-censorship — a preview for the many states copying Ohio's higher-education overhaul.

title: Billionaire Jeff Yass pours $10 million into PAC backing Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy
why: A single $10 million check from Pennsylvania investor Jeff Yass now bankrolls the main PAC behind GOP gubernatorial frontrunner Vivek Ramaswamy, a vivid example of how a handful of megadonors can dominate a statewide race — a dynamic playing out in governor's contests across the country.

title: Pennsylvania's fatal overdose prosecutions divide grieving families
why: Pennsylvania prosecutors increasingly charge those who supplied a fatal dose with drug-delivery-resulting-in-death, and the practice is splitting grieving families — some demand the charges, others say they jail fellow users instead of confronting addiction.

title: West Virginians won local control over landfills decades ago. Now they want it over data centers.
why: A new state law strips counties of zoning, noise and lighting authority over hyperscale data centers and routes most of the tax revenue to the state — echoing a 1980s fight over landfills and previewing the local-versus-state clashes erupting as the AI data-center boom lands in communities across the country.

title: Cherry and Iron wildfires top 71,000 acres as Utah towns evacuate again
why: Two wind-driven wildfires near Eureka and St. George burned past 71,000 combined acres, forcing repeat evacuations and prompting “last resort” power shut-offs that left towns dark — what Gov. Spencer Cox called some of the worst fire conditions in Utah’s history as the drought-stricken West heads into a dangerous summer.

title: 23,000 acres of Ohio public land up for fracking in upcoming votes
why: State officials are deciding whether to open roughly 23,000 acres of publicly owned wildlife areas, including Jockey Hollow and Egypt Valley, to oil-and-gas drilling — a high-stakes test of how much of Ohio’s public land gets leased to frackers over the objections of conservation groups.

title: Why New York’s ‘precision policing’ raises civil rights concerns
why: A close look at the NYPD’s data-driven “precision policing” shows how targeting small groups deemed likely to commit violence can sweep up people based on who they know rather than what they’ve done — a model spreading to other departments that advocates warn deepens surveillance of Black and Latino neighborhoods.

title: Florida’s notorious ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ immigration detention center is now closed
why: The remote Everglades detention camp that became a national symbol of harsh immigration enforcement has shut down, a reversal that changes where hundreds of detainees are held and sharpens scrutiny of the conditions migrants endured there.

title: Cornyn opposes Texas Republicans’ push to close GOP primaries
why: Sen. John Cornyn broke with Gov. Greg Abbott and AG Ken Paxton over a plan to bar independents from voting in Republican primaries, warning it would shrink the party — a fight over who gets to vote that is playing out in other one-party-dominated states.

title: Missoula delays security camera upgrade over AI surveillance concerns
why: The City Council held off on buying new park surveillance cameras after residents raised alarms about AI-powered facial recognition and tracking, opting to write a governing policy first — a local test of how cities set guardrails on surveillance tech before deploying it.

title: Wyoming designates its first-ever protected pronghorn migration corridor
why: Gov. Mark Gordon approved the nation’s first fully designated pronghorn migration route at the 6,000-year-old Trapper’s Point crossing, a precedent other Western states are likely to weigh as they try to balance energy and development against the big-game migrations their ecosystems depend on.

title: Haitian families brace for deportation after Supreme Court TPS ruling
why: After the Supreme Court let the administration end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians, families who have worked legally and built lives in the U.S. could lose their status overnight — a wrenching shift for hundreds of thousands of people and the communities and employers that rely on them.

title: Mississippi’s soaring prison rate could be curbed by a real public defender system, official says
why: Mississippi is among the few states with no statewide public defender system, and a state official argues that building one could ease one of the nation’s highest incarceration rates — a structural gap that keeps poor defendants jailed longer and that other underfunded states share.

title: DeWine vetoes bill requiring photo ID for mail voting in Ohio
why: Republican Gov. Mike DeWine vetoed a GOP-backed measure to require photo ID for absentee ballots, siding with seniors, disabled voters and students who rely on mail voting and setting up a clash with his own party over ballot access heading into the November election.

title: Former Mississippi state Sen. Philip Moran and son sentenced for bribery
why: Ex-state Sen. Philip Moran and his son, a former Diamondhead councilman, were sent to prison for bribery and conspiracy, a rare corruption conviction of a sitting-era Mississippi lawmaker that signals prosecutors’ willingness to pursue Gulf Coast political graft.

title: Glacier National Park employees vote to unionize
why: Workers at Glacier and 11 other National Park Service sites across the West voted 317-11 to unionize after the Trump administration’s deep Park Service cuts, a rare labor win on federal public lands that could give rangers leverage over staffing and safety as visitation peaks.

title: Judge blocks Tennessee mandate to report undocumented families seeking children’s care
why: A court temporarily blocked Tennessee from forcing doctors to report the immigration status of families using Children’s Special Services, a program for kids with serious medical needs — a fight over whether immigration enforcement can be wired into children’s health care that other states are watching.

title: Supreme Court ends protected status for thousands of CT Haitians
why: The U.S. Supreme Court let the Trump administration end Temporary Protected Status for roughly 1.3 million immigrants, including Haitians and Syrians, exposing longtime residents who have worked legally for years to sudden deportation — a ruling whose fallout will hit immigrant communities in every state, with Connecticut’s large Haitian population among the first to feel it.

title: Santa Clara County and state seek immediate halt to ICE facility
why: California’s attorney general and Santa Clara County asked a federal court to stop construction of a 150-bed immigration detention center near Gilroy, testing how far local and state governments can go to block ICE expansion on their own turf.

title: Supreme Court clears way for Trump to revive restrictive asylum policy
why: The justices cleared the path to reinstate “metering,” which caps how many migrants can seek asylum each day at the U.S.-Mexico border, a change that will quickly reshape conditions at El Paso and other crossings and could strand thousands of asylum seekers in Mexican border cities.

title: Utah’s Cottonwood Fire grows to 70,000 acres near Beaver
why: The fast-moving Cottonwood Fire ballooned to roughly 70,000 acres near Beaver, forcing evacuations and straining crews as an unusually dry, hot stretch primes the Intermountain West for a destructive wildfire season.

title: Mayor creates Gun Violence Reduction Office, but critics question its impact
why: Mayor Brandon Johnson signed an executive order creating an Office of Gun Violence Reduction as a step toward a permanent department, but anti-violence workers question whether a new bureaucracy will actually reach the neighborhoods hit hardest by shootings.

title: What 911 calls reveal about jails in St. Louis, Cleveland and Jackson
why: By obtaining 911 logs that local officials tried to keep secret, reporters documented surges of emergency calls — medical crises, suicide attempts, fires and assaults — that expose patterns of neglect inside three city jails, offering a replicable method other newsrooms can use to pierce jail secrecy nationwide.

title: Legislative committee probes Montana Lottery audit report
why: A state accountant told lawmakers the Montana Lottery’s books were off by $18.5 million over several years because its former financial-services director stopped doing his job before his 2025 death; auditors found no fraud but a breakdown of internal controls in an agency that funnels revenue to the state.

title: Families, patients of disabled Kentuckians demand renewed clinic funding at hearing
why: Kentuckians with intellectual and developmental disabilities packed a Frankfort hearing to fight cuts that will force the Lee Specialty Clinic to slash outpatient care in July, eliminating services for more than 1,000 of the state’s most medically vulnerable residents.

title: Mexican man dies in ICE custody in Laredo, at least the 20th fatality this year
why: A Mexican man died in ICE custody at a Laredo detention center — at least the 20th death in immigration detention nationwide this year and the fifth in Texas — intensifying scrutiny of medical care and oversight as ICE holds record numbers of detainees.

title: Final report on NES winter storm response cites flaws, suggests changes
why: An outside after-action report found Nashville Electric Service botched its response to a winter storm that knocked out power to half its customers, faulting emergency planning, public communication and crew coordination — and laying out fixes before the next disaster.

title: Utah officials warn of ‘totally unprecedented’ water shortages as towns run dry
why: Wells and streams are running dry and Utah towns face cutoffs as Lake Powell nears a record low and the seven Colorado River states stay deadlocked over how to share a shrinking supply — a water crisis rippling well beyond Utah across the entire basin.

title: Trump administration sues New York over its immigration package
why: The Trump administration sued New York over its new immigrant-protection laws, escalating a federal-versus-state showdown over sanctuary policies whose outcome could set precedent for how far Washington can force local cooperation with ICE.

title: Colorado won federal approval to import prescription drugs from Canada. Now comes the hard part.
why: After seven years of applications, Colorado won federal approval to import lower-cost prescription drugs from Canada — a first-in-the-nation green light that other states pursuing the same path will watch closely as a real-world test of whether importation can actually lower drug prices.

title: Ohio nursing home chain Arbors repeatedly accused of deadly neglect

The visit previews a national fight over dismantling the Education Department.

title: Reacting to Supreme Court, NC House wants to limit tourism occupancy tax spending
why: Responding to a state Supreme Court ruling, NC House members advanced a bill June 2 to bar counties from spending hotel occupancy taxes on public safety and core services, targeting Currituck County's use of the money. It tests how tourism-reliant counties can fund basic services.

title: Thousands to lose Medi-Cal and food aid in Santa Clara County
why: New federal work requirements that took effect June 1 now reach adults up to age 64; UC Berkeley estimates 129,000 Santa Clara County residents will lose Medi-Cal by 2028, with CalFresh recipients also exposed. The same One Big Beautiful Bill Act rules are squeezing safety-net families in every AJP region.

title: Colorado officials call for more state actions to combat impacts of drought
why: Members of Colorado's Drought Task Force urged Gov. Jared Polis on June 2 to issue an emergency proclamation to unlock aid as worsening drought grips the state. With record-early snowmelt across the West, the plea signals how strained water and wildfire conditions are becoming region-wide.

title: Metro's Gallatin Pike plans paused for Choose How You Move
why: Nashville officials drew backlash June 2 after pausing safety redesigns for Main Street and Gallatin Pike, two of the city's deadliest corridors, under its Choose How You Move program. Advocates say the delay leaves pedestrians exposed on roads with a history of fatal crashes.

title: Missouri's drive to eliminate income tax leaves KC-area officials with more questions than answers
why: Missouri's push to phase out its income tax leaves Kansas City-area officials unsure how to backfill the services that depend on state revenue, the Beacon reported June 2. Several states are racing to scrap income taxes, and the local fallout here is a preview for all of them.

title: Progressive blogger arrested outside Ohio statehouse
why: DJ Byrnes, founder of the progressive blog The Rooster, was arrested at the Ohio Statehouse and charged with telecommunications harassment over messages to a state senator he routinely mocks, in a story updated June 2. Free-speech advocates warn the case could signal officials punishing political criticism.

title: As Ned Lamont touts record, Josh Elliott's campaign strengthens
why: Challenger Josh Elliott cleared the fundraising threshold to qualify for a $3.75 million public grant, sharpening his Democratic primary fight with Gov. Ned Lamont, CT Mirror reported June 2. The race tests whether a well-funded progressive can pull an incumbent governor leftward.

title: Federal judge blocks breakup of NCAR in Boulder, blasting Trump for political revenge on Colorado
why: A judge halted the administration's plan to dismantle Boulder's National Center for Atmospheric Research and hand its supercomputer to the University of Wyoming, calling it retaliation against Colorado. A test of how far courts will check federal payback against blue states.

title: Federal prosecutors tout results of Charlotte crime crackdown
why: Prosecutors charged 56 people and arrested 157 fugitives in a three-month Charlotte surge dubbed Operation Spring Cleaning. The crackdown reflects the Justice Department's expanding use of federal charges to drive local policing.

title: Ohio property tax overhaul signed into law, cutting taxes by billions
why: Gov. DeWine signed bills capping the automatic property-tax increases that come from rising home values, cutting expected future taxes by as much as $3 billion. Relief for homeowners that also squeezes the schools and local services funded by those dollars.

title: Texas lifts ban on CDLs for temporary agriculture workers, drops Spanish-language test option
why: Texas DPS lifted its ban on commercial driver's licenses for immigrants on temporary farm-work visas while scrapping the Spanish-language CDL test, two moves that reshape who can legally drive trucks in the state's economy.

title: Questions about El Paso ISD's financial crisis answered
why: El Paso ISD expects a $52.8 million deficit and may cut about 410 jobs by declaring financial exigency, a rare step that lets a district break employee contracts. Falling enrollment is forcing the same reckoning on school systems across the country.

title: Whistleblower phones were 'blowing up' in Utah state auditor's office after MIDA data center vote, official says
